big: When rates rise, old bonds paying lower rates look less attractive, so their prices fall. A fund holding long bonds feels this more than a fund holding short ones. This lesson explains how funds behave in a hiking cycle. It is not a call on what to buy.

lines: Why would a debt fund lose money when rates go up?
Its bonds are marked to market. If new bonds pay more, old ones are worth less. The longer the bond, the bigger the fall. Short funds hold up better.

q: RBI hikes the repo rate. Which fund type tends to see the larger mark-to-market loss?
why: Money-market funds hold very short paper.
Longer bonds are more sensitive to rate rises.

q: Which of these may feel pressure in a hiking cycle?
opts: Companies with no loans at all, ever
Every sector, in the same way

why: A firm with no loans is less exposed. That does not match this case.
Higher rates raise borrowing costs for these sectors.
Sectors differ in sensitivity. It does not answer what was asked.
Pressure is not limited to gold. The details here point elsewhere.

q: What can rising real rates do to gold?
opts: Fix it at a constant level
Force the RBI to sell it
why: Gold prices move; they are not fixed. It does not fit the facts given.
Rates do not change import duty. It does not answer what was asked.
Gold pays no interest, so higher real rates can weigh on it.

pts: In a hiking cycle, long bond funds face mark-to-market losses.
Short, money-market and floating funds hold up better.
Banks, realty, autos and gold react differently.
